title: Running the Wrong Way
sum: The LORD tells Jonah son of Amittai to go to Nineveh, the great city of Assyria, and call out against its wickedness. Jonah gets up and goes the other way. He goes down to Joppa, pays his fare and boards a ship for Tarshish, as far west as a ship can go. The LORD hurls a great wind onto the sea. The sailors, each with his own god, pray and throw their cargo overboard while Jonah sleeps in the hold.

The sailors wake him, cast lots, and the lot falls on Jonah. He says he is a Hebrew who fears the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land. He tells them to throw him in. They try to row back, then pray to the LORD, hurl Jonah into the sea, and the storm stops. They fear the LORD, offer a sacrifice and make vows. The LORD appoints a huge fish, and it swallows Jonah.
readings: Read as history

A prophet known from 2 Kings 14:25 is sent to a real city and runs. The storm, the lot and the fish are real events in which God steers wind, water and a creature. The sailors' fear and vows are the first sign that the God of Israel is Lord of the nations.
Read as literature

A carefully built story. Words repeat on purpose ("great," "hurl," "fear," "go down"), and the characters are drawn with irony: the prophet who flees and sleeps, the pagan sailors who pray and spare him. The fish arrives like the end of a scene, not an event to be explained.
Read as theology

Nowhere to run: Psalm 139:7-12 turns into a story. God's reach covers the sea, the storm and a foreign crew. The chapter asks what it means to "fear the LORD" when the one who says he does is the one who runs.

views.H: The setting is the 700s BC, in the days of Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25), when Assyria's power was weak and Israel's border was wide. The ship's route, Joppa to Tarshish, is a real trade route on the Mediterranean. Nothing in Assyrian or Phoenician records mentions Jonah.
views.C: Most critical scholars read the book as a story written long after the 700s, in the Persian period. Signs: "God of the heavens" (1:9), words that look late or foreign (the word for "ship" in 1:5, "decree" in 3:7), and the use of the Exodus creed in 4:2. Conservative scholars (Stuart, Alexander) defend an early date.
views.J: Jewish readers asked why Jonah fled. The Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael: he left the land so that the divine presence would not come to him, and feared that the Gentiles would repent and shame Israel. Rashi follows this. Later legends fill in the fish: Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer (about AD 750-850) has Jonah see wonders inside it and the sailors become converts. The book is read on Yom Kippur.
views.X: From the earliest Christians, the three days in the fish were read as a sign of Christ's burial and resurrection (Matthew 12:40). Jerome sees in Jonah's offer to be thrown into the sea a figure of Christ, who gave himself to save others. Jonah's flight is read as a type of Israel, or of the unwilling prophet who becomes the means of the nations' conversion.
views.L: Chapter 1 is the first panel of a two-part story. Chapters 1-2 happen at sea and chapters 3-4 at the city. In each half God commands, the human response varies, a prayer is prayed, and a question is asked. Sasson, Trible and Magonet all lay out the parallels.

deep.b:
Jonah has four short chapters and two halves. The first half (1-2) ends with Jonah praying from the fish and being put on dry land; the second (3-4) begins with the same words as the first, "The word of the LORD came to Jonah" (3:1, compare 1:1). The same pairs appear on each side: a command (1:2; 3:2), a response of the foreigners (the sailors 1:5-16; the Ninevites 3:5-9), a prayer (2:1-9; 4:2-3) and a rescue or a question (2:10; 4:4-11). The narrator never explains. Jonah never speaks to the sailors about his mission; the LORD gives only one reason, Nineveh's wickedness (1:2).

Notice, too, how much of the story is told in dialogue, and how little Jonah says. His one speech (1:9) is a creed, and his one request (1:12) is to be thrown into the sea.

Other prophets protest or hesitate when God calls them: Moses (Exodus 3:11-4:17), Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:6), Elijah (1 Kings 19:3-4). Jonah is the only one who runs. The text does not say why, so the reader waits until 4:2. In the meantime the story lets the reader see a prophet at his worst and foreigners at their best, and then asks the reader which side of the page they are on.

echoes: Genesis 18:20-21; Genesis 10:11-12; Psalm 139:7-12; Joshua 7:14-18; 1 Samuel 14:41-42; Proverbs 16:33; Mark 4:38; Acts 10:5-9; Matthew 12:38-41

settings.to: Jonah son of Amittai, a prophet of the northern kingdom
settings.when: In the days of Jeroboam II, as the story is set (2 Kings 14:23-29)
settings.why: To send a prophet to the capital of Israel's most feared neighbor with a charge against its wickedness. Jonah runs the other way; why he runs is not said until 4:2.
settings.readers: The book's first readers, most likely Judeans in the Persian period (the common view), knew Nineveh as a ruined city and Assyria as the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom. They read about a prophet who ran from his job as a question about themselves.
views: The story is set in the days of Jeroboam II, and the commission is a command to a prophet in Israel when Assyria was weak but dangerous.
Judeans in the 400s-300s BC read the story long after Assyria had fallen, and it speaks to their own question: should we want enemies forgiven?

settings.when: At the height of the storm, after the crew have prayed and thrown the cargo overboard
settings.why: To make every god in the ship work for them: if the foreigner's god is any use, they need him. He is not praying to a doubtful god out of piety but out of fear.
settings.readers: The first readers heard a pagan captain telling a prophet of the LORD to pray. It is the first of several moments when foreigners understand better than Jonah what is at stake.

settings.to: The sailors, who have found him out by lot
settings.when: In the storm, when the crew find the lot has fallen on him
settings.why: To answer their question ("Which people do you belong to?") and to tell them what to do. He says who he is, what he fears, and how to save the ship, without a word of prayer or apology.
settings.readers: Readers were told only that he is a Hebrew who fears the LORD. They had to decide whether this was courage, resignation or irony.
views: Jonah offers his life for the crew, as the Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael and many Christian readers say.
He prefers death to obedience, as he does in 4:3 and 4:8.

settings.when: After rowing hard for shore failed
settings.why: To ask the LORD not to hold them guilty of killing an innocent man if they throw Jonah into the sea. The prayer calls the LORD by name and says he does what he wants.
settings.readers: For the first readers the best prayer in the chapter is the foreigners'. It is also the first time anyone in the story speaks to the LORD by name.

traditions.q: Is Jonah history, a parable, or something else? And what is "the sign of Jonah"?
views: The Church has not defined the book's genre. Dei Verbum 12 tells interpreters to find the literary forms the writers used, and Catholic scholars hold both that Jonah is history and that it is an instructive story. The Church reads the Old Testament's persons and events as types of Christ (Catechism 128-130), and Jonah's three days have long been read as a sign of the burial and resurrection (Matthew 12:40).

The Fathers (Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, Theodoret) read Jonah as history and the three days as a type of Christ's burial and resurrection. Jonah's prayer (2:3-10 in Hebrew numbering) is sung as the Sixth Ode of the canons at Matins, and Jonah is one of the Old Testament readings at the Vesperal Liturgy of Holy Saturday.

Luther's lectures on Jonah (1525-26) read the book as history. He takes the fish as one of God's miracles, linked as Jesus links it to the resurrection (Matthew 12:40), and Jonah as an example of the Word at work among a people who did not know it.
Calvin's lectures on Jonah treat the book as history and the three days as a type of Christ's burial and resurrection, and take the sign of Jonah as Christ's own interpretation (Matthew 12:40).

Many evangelical scholars (for example Stuart and Alexander) defend Jonah as history and cite Jesus's use of it (Matthew 12:41) and 2 Kings 14:25. Others hold that a parable or didactic story is a legitimate literary form, which an inerrancy statement permits, since the Chicago Statement (Article XVIII) says the text is read according to its literary forms.

Seventh-day Adventist teaching reads Jonah as history. Ellen G. White's Prophets and Kings retells it as the story of a prophet sent to a repentant people, and Adventists often use the book as an example of a prophecy that was conditional.

title: A Psalm from the Deep
sum: From inside the fish Jonah prays a psalm. He remembers calling to the LORD from his trouble and being heard, from the belly of Sheol. He says that God threw him into the deep and that the breakers and waves passed over him. He felt driven from God's sight, yet he looked toward the holy temple. Water closed over him, weeds bound his head, and he went down to the roots of the mountains.

Then comes the turn: "But out of the Pit you brought my life up." He remembered the LORD, and his prayer came to the temple. He says that those who cling to empty nothings give up their loyal love, and he promises a sacrifice of thanks and the payment of his vows. The psalm ends, "Rescue is the LORD's." The LORD speaks to the fish, and it vomits Jonah onto dry land.
readings: Read as a prayer
A prayer of a man who was drowning and has been brought up. The psalm is the rescue's testimony: what it felt like to go down and to be lifted. It says nothing of repentance and little of why.
Read as irony

The only thing Jonah prays is a thanksgiving, in a fish, before he is out. He thanks God for his own rescue and condemns idolaters for abandoning loyal love, yet he fled God and will resent God's loyal love to Nineveh in 4:2.
Read as the community's voice
A psalm made of psalms (Psalm 18, 30, 31, 42, 69, 120), as if the whole worshiping community prays through the prophet. Persian-period readers would have known every line.

views.H: Nothing in the chapter can be dated, and it names no historical person or place. It uses the stock images of Israel's temple prayer and describes drowning in the sea.
views.C: The psalm may be original or inserted. Wolff and others see an addition because the psalm lacks repentance and speaks of rescue in the past, while Landes, Magonet, Sasson and Trible show the psalm fits the story's irony. Its language is close to the Psalms and has no clear pre-exilic markers.
views.J: On Yom Kippur the whole book is read at the afternoon service (Bavli Megillah 31a), and many communities add Micah 7:18-20 after it; the psalm of rescue fits the day when Israel asks forgiveness. Jewish commentators read it as Jonah's prayer of thanks. Later midrash adds that the fish had eyes like windows and showed Jonah the depths (a legend).
views.X: The fathers read the fish as the tomb and the psalm as the voice of the Savior from Sheol, the voice of Christ in his descent. The Orthodox sing it as the Sixth Ode. A third strand (Calvin) stresses that Jonah is an example of a believer praying in the depths.
views.L: The prayer is the book's center and its contradiction. It is the longest speech in the book, in verse where everything else is prose, and the only place where Jonah praises God. Critics argue about whether it is Jonah's finest moment or his most self-satisfied.

deep.h: The Hebrew behind the verse numbers
deep.b: In English, chapter 1 ends with the huge fish and chapter 2 has ten verses. In printed Hebrew Bibles, the fish is 2:1 and the prayer runs 2:2-10, with a final verse 2:11. This site follows the English numbers. See the note on 1:17.

Almost every line of the prayer matches a line in the Psalter. Jonah 2:2 echoes Psalm 120:1 and Psalm 18:6; 2:3, Psalm 42:7; 2:4, Psalm 31:22; 2:5, Psalm 69:1-2; 2:6, Psalm 30:3; 2:8, Psalm 31:6; 2:9, Psalm 50:14 and Psalm 3:8. Some think the writer composed the prayer from the psalms he knew; others think the psalm is older and was set into the story. Either way the reader hears familiar words in a new mouth.
deep.refs: Psalm 120:1; Psalm 18:6; Psalm 42:7; Psalm 31:22; Psalm 69:1-2; Psalm 30:3; Psalm 31:6; Psalm 50:14; Psalm 3:8

echoes: Psalm 120:1; Psalm 18:4-6; Psalm 42:7; Psalm 31:22; Psalm 69:1-2; Psalm 30:3; Psalm 31:6; Psalm 3:8; Matthew 12:40; Hosea 6:2

settings.when: From inside the fish, during the three days (1:17), before it vomits him out
settings.why: To give thanks for being brought up from the Pit alive. A thanksgiving, not a petition: Jonah speaks as if the rescue were done.
settings.readers: Persian-period Judeans who sang these psalms in the temple heard a worshiper's song made of psalms they knew. They also heard what the book does not say: no repentance, no change of heart toward Nineveh.
views: An original part of the story
The psalm is the book's turning point and mirrors the prayer in 4:2-3 (Landes, Magonet, Sasson, Trible).
The psalm interrupts the narrative from 1:17 to 2:10 and does not mention the fish or the sailors (Wolff and others).

title: Forty Days
sum: The word of the LORD comes to Jonah a second time, and this time he goes. Nineveh is a city great in God's eyes, a walk of three days. Jonah goes one day's walk into it and calls out, "Forty days more, and Nineveh will be overturned!" The people of Nineveh believe in God. They call a fast, and from the greatest to the least they put on sackcloth.

When word reaches the king, he takes off his robe, puts on sackcloth and sits in the ashes. By his decree, no one, human or animal, may eat or drink. All are to call out to God and turn back from their evil way and the violence in their hands. "Who knows?" he says. "God may turn and change his mind." God sees what they do. He changes his mind about the harm, and he does not do it.
readings: Read as history

A real mission to a real city. The Ninevites responded to a prophet's warning as other nations in Scripture did, and God showed mercy as Jeremiah 18:7-8 says he will. Some commentators suggest that the plagues and the eclipse recorded in the Assyrian eponym lists (765-759 BC) could have left the city anxious; no text connects them to Jonah.
Read as satire or parable

The city is too large, the king too quick, the animals in sackcloth comic. The story exaggerates so that the reader sees that even the most hardened enemy responds to God more readily than God's own prophet.
Read as teaching on repentance

The chapter shows how repentance works: believe, fast, turn from violence, hope without presuming ("Who knows?"). God answers by changing his mind, which Jeremiah 18:7-10 says is how his warnings work.

views.H: The story is placed in the days of Jeroboam II, when Ashur-dan III (772-755 BC) ruled Assyria. The Assyrian eponym lists record plague in 765 and 759 BC and a solar eclipse in 763 BC; some commentators suggest these omens could have made a city receptive to a warning. No Assyrian text names Jonah or a king's public repentance.
views.C: The past tense of "Nineveh was a city great in God's eyes" (3:3), a king of Nineveh not named, the hyperbole of three days and of animals fasting, and the lack of any Assyrian record point most critics to a late, partly fictional story. Others (Stuart, Alexander) hold that these features fit a real mission.
views.J: The Ninevites' repentance is the model for Yom Kippur. The Mishnah (Ta'anit 2:1) uses 3:10 in the liturgy for fast days: it is not said that God saw their sackcloth and fasting, but that he saw their deeds, that they turned from their evil way. The Mekhilta and Rashi tell how Jonah feared Gentile repentance would shame Israel.
views.X: Jesus says the people of Nineveh will rise at the judgment and condemn his generation, because they repented at Jonah's preaching (Matthew 12:41; Luke 11:32). Augustine reads "Nineveh overturned" as the overthrow of wickedness in the converted. The Ethiopian, Coptic and Syriac churches keep a Fast of Nineveh before Lent.
views.L: The chapter is the mirror of chapter 1: a second call, a prophet who obeys, foreigners who respond at once, and a king who does what the sailors did and more. It is the book's only plain happy ending, and the next chapter turns it into a problem.

deep.b: Outside the Bible, no text tells of a repentance of Nineveh in the 700s BC. Assyrian records show that kings did take omens, eclipses and plague seriously, sometimes with a substitute king and rites of mourning. The Assyrian eponym lists (Millard, The Eponyms of the Assyrian Empire) record a plague in 765 and 759 BC and an eclipse in 763 BC. Commentators sometimes link these with the story; no ancient text does. Nineveh's later history was not one of repentance: Nahum celebrates its fall in 612 BC, and Matthew 12:41 uses the Ninevites as a standard for later hearers.

The Hebrew verb in Jonah's sermon, hapakh, describes both the overthrow of Sodom and a change from one state to another. Jonah means the first; what happens is the second. The reader is invited to see that the prophecy came true in the sense that mattered. Jerome and Augustine took that point. The Greek translators, who wrote "three days" for "forty" (see the variant), also chose a verb that means "be overthrown."

deep.title: Claude's theory: the five-word sermon
deep.b: Jonah's whole sermon is five words in Hebrew, with no mention of God's name, no offer of mercy and no call to repent. The people respond as if God had said all of it. My reading: the narrator wants the reader to see that the response is not Jonah's doing. The words work, but the credit goes to God, as the king's "Who knows?" shows. This overlaps published readings that stress the sermon's brevity and Jonah's unwillingness (Sasson, Trible), and the idea that the narrative gives God, not the prophet, the success.

echoes: Genesis 19:25; Deuteronomy 29:23; Jeremiah 18:7-10; Jeremiah 26:3; Joel 2:12-14; 2 Samuel 12:22; Exodus 32:14; Matthew 12:41; Luke 11:32

settings.to: The people of Nineveh, in the city, walking in for a day
settings.when: After the second call, in the city (three days across, or a three-day visit)
settings.why: To announce that the city will be overturned in forty days. The message has no stated condition and no offer of mercy; the Ninevites take it as a warning to which they may respond.
settings.readers: The first readers knew that Nineveh was destroyed in 612 BC and that Jonah's warning was not carried out. They read about a warning that worked.
views: A warning with a hidden condition
The rule of Jeremiah 18:7-10: a threatened disaster is canceled if the nation turns back.
Jonah's five words fail as prophecy; in this reading he is right to be angry (4:2).

settings.by: The king of Nineveh and his great men
settings.to: All the people and animals of Nineveh
settings.when: As soon as the news reaches him, on the first days of Jonah's warning
settings.why: To lead the whole city in fasting and repentance: no food or drink, sackcloth for everyone and the animals, a cry to God and a turning from violence. The king gives them a hope, not a promise: "Who knows?"
settings.readers: Readers in the Persian period saw a pagan king doing what Judah's own kings (Ahab, Hezekiah) did when a prophet spoke. It is also the model of a decree that does not presume on mercy.

traditions.q: Does God really change his mind (3:10; 4:2)?
views: God does not change in his being or purpose; Scripture speaks of his "repenting" in human terms (the Westminster Confession says he is without body, parts or passions and unchangeable, 2.1). Calvin reads 3:10 as God changing his outward action while his eternal purpose stands.

Luther says God's "repenting" is a way of speaking: God remains the same while the people change and so meet him differently. For Lutherans the stress falls on God's word as law and gospel, and the Ninevites meet the second.
Aquinas teaches that God's will is immutable even when it wills changes in creatures; the language of "repentance" describes the effect, not a change in God (Summa Theologiae I, q. 19, a. 7).

The Fathers teach that God is unchangeable, and that Scripture speaks of his repentance in human language, out of his condescension (Chrysostom's synkatabasis); it is people who turn and so find a different God than they feared.

Wesleyan and Arminian teachers stress that God's warnings are conditional and his responses real. John Wesley's notes on the Old Testament read God's turning from the threatened punishment as the answer to the Ninevites' repentance.

Many evangelicals hold the classical view (God is unchanging and the language is figurative). Open theists, a minority among evangelicals, argue that God really does respond and change course, and cite Jonah 3:10 as a main text (The Openness of God, 1994).

traditions.q: What does Nineveh's repentance say about people outside Israel (3:5-10)?
views: Lumen Gentium 16 teaches that those who through no fault of their own do not know the Gospel but seek God sincerely may attain salvation by his grace. Catholic readers cite Nineveh and Matthew 12:41 as a sign of God's mercy to the nations.

Orthodox teaching holds that God's mercy is for all people and leaves the judgment of any person to him; the Church does not define the fate of those outside it. The Ninevites' turning (metanoia) is held up as a pattern for the Church's own repentance, and Jesus's words in Matthew 12:41 are read as a warning to the hearers.
Luther reads "the people of Nineveh believed in God" as true faith in God's word, which gives forgiveness; salvation is by faith alone, wherever the Word is heard.

The Westminster Confession (10.4) says people who do not profess the Christian religion cannot be saved in any other way; Reformed readers take the Ninevites' repentance as a gift of God given through the word preached, and Acts 11:18 as the pattern.

Evangelicals divide. Exclusivists hold that explicit faith in Christ is needed and take Nineveh as a temporary reprieve; inclusivists such as Clark Pinnock (A Wideness in God's Mercy, 1992) argue that God's mercy reaches people who respond to the light they have, as Peter says in Acts 10:34-35.

traditions.q: Should a community fast when it repents (3:5-8)?
views: Fasting is one of the three ways of repentance named in Scripture and the Fathers, with prayer and almsgiving (Catechism 1434). Jonah 3 is read in the Roman liturgy during Lent.

As church practice (the sources are liturgical calendars, not a confession), the Coptic Church keeps the three-day Fast of Jonah and the Syriac churches the Rogation of the Ninevites, before Lent, in memory of the Ninevites' fast.
As church practice (the source is the church's liturgical calendar), the Ethiopian church keeps the Fast of Nineveh (Tsome Nenewe), three days before Great Lent, and reads Jonah in it.
The Reformed churches have called days of public fasting in times of crisis and have not tied fasting to a fixed season; the Second Helvetic Confession (chapter 24) teaches that fasts are free.

Common Baptist practice, not a confessional rule: fasting is voluntary and personal or congregational; Baptist teaching generally holds that no day is fixed by Scripture, and Jonah 3 is read as an example of a community's turning, not of an obligation.

title: Is It Right to Be Angry?
sum: Jonah is furious. He prays: this is why he ran, because he knew the LORD was gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, great in loyal love, and one who changes his mind about the harm. He asks to die. The LORD asks, "Are you right to burn with anger?" Jonah leaves the city, builds a booth east of it and waits to see what will happen.

The LORD God appoints a leafy plant to shade him, and Jonah rejoices. Next morning God appoints a worm, which kills the plant, and a hot east wind. Jonah begs to die again. God asks him whether he is right to burn with anger over the plant. "Even to death," says Jonah. The LORD answers: you had pity on a plant you did not make; "should I not have pity on Nineveh, the great city," with its 120,000 people who do not know their right hand from their left, and many animals? The book ends with the question.
readings: Read as a rebuke
God shows the prophet up. Jonah wanted Israel's God to be small. The plant shows that his pity is for himself and his comfort.
Read as an open question
The book ends with a question the reader must answer. Jonah does not reply because the reader is Jonah.
Read as a lesson on God's character
The creed is true, even for Assyria. God's mercy does not depend on the nation, and a prophet's embarrassment is not a reason to hold it back.

views.H: The scene is outside Nineveh. History offers little: Nineveh was destroyed in 612 BC, as Nahum announces, and Assyria had conquered Samaria in 722/721 BC. The book's question about pity for an enemy is one it asks of its Judean readers.
views.C: The creed in 4:2 matches Exodus 34:6-7 and Joel 2:13, and critics date the book after those texts. The plant's name (qiqayon) is rare. The ending is thought to be deliberately open; the Greek and Hebrew agree on it.
views.J: Radak and Rashi take Jonah's anger as concern for his reputation (if the prophecy did not come true, he would be thought false) or for Israel (Mekhilta). The Yom Kippur haftarah ends here, and many communities add Micah 7:18-20, which praises the God who passes over sin. Jewish readers treat Jonah's anger as the foil to God's pardon.
views.X: Jerome's commentary gives allegorical readings alongside the plain sense, and he and Augustine argued by letter over the plant's name (gourd or ivy). Jonah's anger has been read as Israel's, though modern scholars warn that this makes Judaism the villain and misreads a Jewish book written for Jews. The book's ending is read with Acts 10:34-35 and Matthew 28:19.
views.L: The chapter is the book's final joke and its final question. It has three "appointments" (the plant, the worm and the wind), two "great" words (evil and joy) and an argument from the small to the great. The ending leaves Jonah on the hillside and the reader in his place.

deep.b: Jonah quotes the LORD's own words from Sinai (Exodus 34:6-7) as a reason he did not want to come to Nineveh. The creed is true, he says, and he knew it. What he leaves out is the second half of Exodus 34:7, that the LORD does not clear the guilty, and he adds "changes his mind about the harm," as Joel 2:13 does. The book makes no secret that the speaker is bitter. It leaves the reader to see that the truth of a creed is no guard against using it wrongly.

deep.h: The old reading of Jonah as Israel
deep.b: For centuries Christian preachers read Jonah as "Israel," narrow and unwilling to share God's mercy with the nations. The book itself gives no sign of this reading. Jonah is one prophet, and the book was written for a Jewish audience, whose own tradition (as the Yom Kippur reading shows) took it as a story about repentance and divine mercy that applies to every reader. The reading also has a harmful history in Christian preaching against Jews; churches have since repudiated that use of Scripture, in the spirit of the Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate 4, which says the Jews are not to be presented as rejected or accursed by God (it does not mention Jonah). The Plain English Translation does not use it.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the plant is a second fish
deep.b: The plant plays the role the fish played in chapter 2. Each rescues Jonah, each is God's appointment, and each is undone or ended so that Jonah learns. The fish rescued him from drowning and he prayed thanks; the plant rescues him from heat and he is glad. But only the fish sends him back to work. This overlaps with Magonet's and Trible's parallel readings of the two halves; the pairing of fish and plant is mine.

echoes: Exodus 34:6-7; Joel 2:13-14; Numbers 11:15; 1 Kings 19:4; Psalm 103:8; Psalm 145:8; Psalm 36:6; Micah 7:18-20; Acts 10:34-35; Matthew 28:19

settings.why: To say why he ran: he knew God would forgive. He asks to die. It is the only time Jonah speaks to God as he feels, and he does so by quoting God's own creed.
settings.readers: The first readers heard their own creed (Exodus 34:6-7; Joel 2:13) in the mouth of a prophet who hates it. The prayer is the book's confession of the reader's problem.
views: Jonah as a type of an unwilling Israel
A reading with a long history in Christian preaching (see the box below on why the text gives no sign of it).
The reader is the one being questioned.

settings.to: Jonah, sitting east of the city, and so to the reader
settings.when: Under the shelter, then in the heat after the plant dies
settings.why: To show Jonah, by a plant and a worm, that he is angry about the wrong loss. A shoot he never planted matters to him; a city of 120,000 and its animals should matter more to God.
settings.readers: The book ends with a question put to Jonah and, through him, to Judeans who had to decide how to feel about Assyria, Babylon and Persia. The ending does not tell them what to say.
